frase_gancho.texto: A courtyard of carved pillars where the eyes once had obsidian pupils, and perhaps these are not butterflies at all.

puente_narrativo.texto: If you are following the full route, cross the passage at the back toward the adjoining courtyards where jaguars sound conch shells; if you are on the express route, when you leave the palace you can listen to the two final stops on the fall and the legacy of the city.

guion_corto.texto: Head to the southwest corner of the Plaza de la Luna and enter by the stairway into this roofed complex. You are inside the Palace of Quetzalpapálotl, one of the best-preserved complexes in Teotihuacán. Walk on to its central courtyard, surrounded by four porticoes held up by square pillars of carved stone. Step up to one of the pillars and look at the bas-relief: the feathers and the head are seen in profile, and the chest from the front. When it was discovered, in nineteen sixty-two, it was thought to be a quetzal with the body of a butterfly. Hence its name in Nahuatl: quetzalli, precious feather, and papálotl, butterfly.

guion_largo.texto:
Now look at the circles on the pillars. Today they seem empty, but in one of them four circles preserved inlays of polished black obsidian, and in one eye its obsidian is still there. The pillars were also carved and inlaid with mica. When light entered the courtyard, the stone must have shone and returned the gaze of anyone passing by.

And here there is a twist. The butterfly name comes from how the images were read when they were discovered, in nineteen sixty-two. Today some scholars propose that the creatures are not quetzal-butterflies, but owls, a symbol of warriors, priests and the Teotihuacán elite. It is an interpretation, and the name stayed out of habit.

Some motifs on these pillars, such as a zigzag band, also appear in murals at Tepantitla, Tetitla, Techinantitla and the Palace of the Jaguars. That suggests that the different complexes of the city shared a common language of images.

Beneath where you are standing there is another building. The Temple of the Feathered Conches, from around the year two hundred, was buried completely beneath this palace and was found intact. Its pillars bear conches with feathers, and its base shows painted birds, probably green macaws.

What was this palace for? It is usually called a house of priests, but some researchers suggest it may have been a meeting place. Perhaps it was linked to a new political movement or to a new ruler. These were the fourth to sixth centuries, when the influence of Teotihuacán reached as far as Maya cities such as Tikal. It is a hypothesis.

The archaeologist Jorge Acosta excavated and reconstructed this complex in the sixties, and published his study of the palace in nineteen sixty-four. In two thousand nine, a conservation project removed the old cement and restored the palace with lime, clay and sand. Today it reads as what it was: a construction of lime with pigment, and not of cement.

texto: Look closely at one of the courtyard pillars to see how the profile of the quetzal bird merges with the butterfly chest
Look in the eye sockets of the reliefs for the shiny black discs of polished obsidian
Look at the red and white step-fret patterns on the interior walls and the stepped merlons that crown the courtyard roof

texto.Elementos destacados: Courtyard of the Pillars with bas-reliefs of Quetzalpapálotl, obsidian eyes, murals with step-fret patterns, and merlons bearing the year sign
texto.Origin: Southwest corner of the Plaza de la Luna

texto.pregunta: Myth: The wooden roofs and merlons of the Palace of Quetzalpapálotl have stood intact since pre-Hispanic times.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The stone pillars and low walls lay buried under their own collapse; the archaeologist Jorge Acosta restored the flat roofs in the sixties, following the original remains found on the floor.
